items.title: UN chief calls New START expiration a 'grave moment'

featured_image.name: UN chief calls New START expiration 'grave moment' - Reuters

items.description:
The New START treaty, the last remaining nuclear arms control agreement between the United States and Russia, expired at midnight GMT on Thursday, February 5, leaving the world without binding limits on the two largest nuclear arsenals for the first time in more than half a century.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the expiration "a grave moment for international peace and security" and urged both nations to return to the negotiating table without delay.[1][2][3][4][5]

"For the first time in more than half a century, we face a world without any binding limits on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the Russian Federation and the United States of America—the two States that possess the overwhelming majority of the global stockpile of nuclear weapons," Guterres said in a statement released Wednesday.[2][3][1]

items.title: Gold tops $5,000 as weak jobs data fuels rate-cut hopes

featured_image.name: Gold's record run rolls on with prices surging past $US5,000 ...

items.description:
Gold reclaimed the key $5,000 level on Wednesday, climbing more than 1% to around $5,017 per ounce as safe-haven demand intensified amid rising geopolitical tensions and fresh signs of labor market softness in the United States. The rally marks a rebound for the precious metal after a volatile stretch that saw prices swing from a record high of nearly $5,595 late last month to a sharp plunge below $4,400 just days ago.

The surge comes as U.S. and Iranian officials confirmed high-stakes nuclear talks will take place Friday in Oman, with considerable uncertainty over whether the two sides can bridge wide gaps on Iran's nuclear program, ballistic missiles, and regional activities. Silver followed suit, jumping nearly 10% to around $91 per ounce.[1][2][3]

items.title: Oil prices dip as US and Iran confirm Friday talks in Oman

featured_image.name: US-Iran nuclear talks set for Oman on Friday, Tehran confirms

items.description:
Global oil prices fell on Wednesday evening as Washington and Tehran confirmed they would hold direct negotiations in Oman on Friday, easing fears of imminent conflict between the two nations.

U.S. crude slipped by about 1% to $64.50 per barrel in Asian trading late Wednesday, while Brent fell to approximately $68.49 per barrel, according to Reuters. The decline marked oil's first retreat in three days, following a 4.8% surge in the previous two sessions driven by fears of potential military strikes against the OPEC producer.[1][2][3]

items.title: Oil prices fall as US and Iran confirm Friday talks in Oman

featured_image.name: Trump-Iran latest: US military shoots down Iranian drone as Tehran demands venue change for talks

items.description:
Crude oil prices have swung sharply this week as military confrontations between the United States and Iran collided with diplomatic efforts, with markets reacting first to the collapse and then the revival of nuclear negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

West Texas Intermediate crude fell more than 1% on Thursday after the U.S. and Iran confirmed they will meet in Oman on Friday to discuss Iran's nuclear program, easing fears that recent hostilities could spiral into open conflict. The decline followed a roughly 3% surge the previous day, when the talks appeared on the verge of falling apart.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Engineers propose 50-mile seabed curtain to slow Thwaites melt

featured_image.name: This 'Doomsday Glacier' is melting faster than anyone thought. Now Earth's biggest cities are in danger

items.description:
A consortium of researchers and engineers is proposing to construct an 80-kilometer underwater barrier to shield Antarctica's Thwaites Glacier from the warm ocean currents driving its rapid deterioration. The ambitious Seabed Curtain Project comes as new data gathered from beneath the glacier reveals turbulent, warm waters capable of accelerating ice loss at an alarming rate.

The proposed structure would stand approximately 150 meters high and be anchored to the seabed at a depth of around 650 meters, forming a physical barrier to restrict the influx of warm water that is melting the glacier from below. The project aims to complete deployment by 2040, with an estimated construction cost of $40 to $80 billion and annual maintenance of $1 to $2 billion over its projected 25-year lifespan.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Last U.S.-Russia nuclear arms treaty set to expire Wednesday

featured_image.name: Last Russia-US treaty on nuclear arms control set to expire

items.description:
For the first time in over fifty years, the world's two largest nuclear powers will operate without limitations on their arsenals after the New START treaty expires on February 5, 2026. The lapse of the agreement, signed in 2010, marks the end of decades of arms control diplomacy between Washington and Moscow and raises concerns about a new era of nuclear competition that could also involve China.

The treaty, which capped deployed strategic warheads at 1,550 and delivery systems at 700 for each nation, also required on-site inspections and data exchanges—measures that had been suspended since Russia halted its participation following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.[1][2][3]

items.title: Heavy snowfall cancels training as 2026 Winter Olympics open

featured_image.name: Heavy snowfall prompts cancellation of women’s downhill training at Milan Cortina Olympics

items.description:
As the Milan-Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics prepare for their February 6 opening ceremony, organizers face a climate change paradox: decades of warming have left venues dependent on artificial snow, yet an intense last-minute snowfall has now forced the cancellation of training runs.

The 2026 Games are taking place in a much warmer climate than when Cortina d'Ampezzo last hosted in 1956, highlighting the growing challenge of staging winter sports in an era of rising global temperatures.
